newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bomb scare at hotel interrupts Hebron talks.
newsitem.headline: Bomb scare at hotel interrupts Hebron talks.

text.p: Israeli-Palestinian peace talks were interrupted on Monday when an anonymous caller said a bomb had been planted at the Jerusalem hotel where they were held, police said.

At 9.30 p.m. (1930 GMT) security guards evacuated U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington, and Palestinian negotiators Mahmoud Abbas and Saeb Erakat from the Laromme hotel, witnesses said.
Israeli police brought in a bomb squad with dogs who searched the grounds for explosives, witnesses said.
"A German-speaking man called the hotel switchboard saying there was a bomb at the hotel," a police spokeswoman said. "Police are checking everything."
A U.S. official said: "There was a bomb scare. They asked us to evacuate the hotel and we are going back as soon as the police tell us to."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told a group of U.S. rabbis in Jerusalem he hoped the long-overdue accord would be concluded shortly.
"This is something I find necessary to say now on the eve, the possible eve of the signing of an agreement," he said, explaining the Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

"It is too early to say if it will be concluded. We need patience. We have plenty of patience. I will sign an agreement when I am convinced that our goals have been reached and I am convinced we will achieve our goals."

Netanyahu, citing security concerns, has delayed implementing the 1995 Israel-PLO agreement on redeployment of Israeli troops in the West Bank since he unseated Shimon Peres's Labour-led coalition in May 1996 elections.

Israel is to hand to the Palestinian Authority 80 percent of Hebron where 400 Jews live and study among 100,000 Arabs. Netanyahu's government has been negotiating with the Palestinians on increasing security for the Jews of Hebron.

Palestinian negotiators attended an emergency cabinet meeting in Gaza during a recess in talks with the Israelis, hours before the bomb scare. The cabinet said in a statement at the end of the meeting:
"The Palestinian leadership will remain in constant meetings to follow up negotiations in the hope to conclude the drafting of the agreement as soon as possible."
A U.S. official said Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was considering returning to Washington on Tuesday after weeks of mediating between Israel and the PLO if the agreement was not finished by then.

Mediation on Sunday by Jordan's King Hussein removed a key negotiating block. Under the compromise -- proposed by both Egypt and Jordan -- Israel will complete three troop withdrawals from other, mostly rural occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.
The PLO had been reluctant to sign an accord without a commitment from Israel to carry out the additional West Bank pullbacks agreed in previous peace deals.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai predicted on Monday that the Hebron deal would be signed on Tuesday.
"I predict this accord will be signed tomorrow," Mordechai told Israel Television. "The army is ready, all the plans have been completed and in a very very short time we can redeploy."
News of an imminent agreement angered members of Netanyahu's right-wing cabinet and Jewish settler leaders who want to hold on to the lands occupied since the 1967 Middle East war.

At least seven ministers in Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet were expected to oppose the deal. Jewish settlers warned the handover would lead to bloodshed in the town holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
